{{short description|Gravity theories that are invariant under Weyl transformations}}
'''Conformal gravity''' refers to gravity theories that are invariant under [[Conformal map|conformal transformations]] in the [[Riemannian geometry]] sense; more accurately, they are invariant under [[Weyl transformation]]s <math>g_{ab}\rightarrow\Omega^2(x)g_{ab}</math> where <math>g_{ab}</math> is the [[metric tensor]] and <math>\Omega(x)</math> is a function on [[spacetime]].

==Weyl-squared theories==
The simplest theory in this category has the square of the [[Weyl tensor]] as the [[Lagrangian (field theory)|Lagrangian]]

:<math>\mathcal{S}=\int \, \mathrm{d}^4x \, \sqrt{-g \;} \, C_{abcd}\,C^{abcd}~,</math>

where <math>\; C_{abcd} \;</math> is the Weyl tensor. This is to be contrasted with the usual [[Einstein–Hilbert action]] where the Lagrangian is just the [[Scalar curvature|Ricci scalar]]. The equation of motion upon varying the metric is called the [[Bach tensor]],

:<math>2\,\partial_a\,\partial_d\,{{C^a}_{bc}}^d ~~+~~ R_{ad} \, {{C^a}_{bc}}^d ~=~ 0~,</math>

where <math>\; R_{ab} \;</math> is the [[Ricci curvature|Ricci tensor]]. Conformally flat metrics are solutions of this equation.

Since these theories lead to [[Quartic function|fourth-order equations]] for the fluctuations around a fixed background, they are not manifestly unitary. It has therefore been generally believed that they could not be consistently quantized. This is now disputed.<ref>

==Four-derivative theories==
Conformal gravity is an example of a 4-[[derivative]] theory. This means that each term in the [[wave equation]] can contain up to four derivatives. There are pros and cons of 4-derivative theories. The pros are that the quantized version of the theory is more convergent and [[renormalization|renormalisable]]. The cons are that there may be issues with [[causality]]. A simpler example of a 4-derivative wave equation is the scalar 4-derivative wave equation:

:<math>
\operatorname{\Box}^2 \Phi =0
</math>

The solution for this in a central field of force is:

:<math>
\Phi(r)= 1 - \frac{2m}{r} +ar +br^2
</math>

The first two terms are the same as a normal wave equation. Because this equation is a simpler approximation to conformal gravity, m corresponds to the mass of the central source. The last two terms are unique to 4-derivative wave equations. It has been suggested that small values be assigned to them to account for the [[Accelerating expansion of the universe|galactic acceleration constant]] (also known as [[dark matter]]) and the [[dark energy]] constant.<ref name='56 (2006) 340-445'>{{cite journal|title=Alternatives to Dark Matter and Dark Energy|journal=Prog. Part. Nucl. Phys.|year=2006|first=Philip D.|last=Mannheim|volume=56|issue=2|pages=340–445|doi= 10.1016/j.ppnp.2005.08.001|arxiv=astro-ph/0505266|bibcode = 2006PrPNP..56..340M |s2cid=14024934}}</ref> The solution equivalent to the [[Schwarzschild metric|Schwarzschild solution]] in [[general relativity]] for a spherical source for conformal gravity has a metric with:

:<math>
\varphi(r) = g^{00}  = (1-6bc)^\frac{1}{2} - \frac{2b}{r} + c r + \frac{d}{3} r^2 
</math>
to show the difference between general relativity. 6bc is very small, and so can be ignored. The additional parameters have been argued to explain [[Galactic rotation curve|galactic rotation curves]] without invoking dark matter.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mannheim |first1=Phillip |last2=O'Brien |first2=James |title=Fitting galactic rotation curves with conformal gravity and a global quadratic potential |journal=Phys. Rev. D |date=June 12, 2012 |volume=85 |issue=12 |article-number=124020 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.85.124020 |url=https://journals.aps.org/prd/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevD.85.124020|arxiv=1011.3495 |bibcode=2012PhRvD..85l4020M }}</ref> 

The main issue with conformal gravity theories, as well as any theory with higher derivatives, is the typical presence of [[Faddeev–Popov ghost#General ghosts in theoretical physics|ghosts]], which point to instabilities of the [[quantum]] version of the theory, although there might be a solution to the ghost problem.<ref name='37:532–571,2007'>{{cite journal|title=Solution to the ghost problem in fourth order derivative theories|journal=Found. Phys.|year=2007|first=Philip D.|last=Mannheim|volume=37|issue=4–5|pages=532–571|arxiv=hep-th/0608154|bibcode = 2007FoPh...37..532M |doi = 10.1007/s10701-007-9119-7 |s2cid=44031727}}</ref>

An alternative approach is to consider the gravitational constant as a [[Spontaneous symmetry breaking|symmetry broken]] [[scalar field]], in which case you would consider a small correction to [[Newton's law of universal gravitation|Newtonian gravity]] like this (where we consider <math>\varepsilon</math> to be a small correction):

:<math>
\operatorname \Box \Phi + \varepsilon^2 \operatorname{\Box}^2 \Phi = 0
</math>

in which case the general solution is the same as the Newtonian case except there can be an additional term:

:<math>
\Phi = 1 - \frac{2m}{r} \left( 1 + \alpha \sin\left(\frac r \varepsilon +\beta\right) \right)
</math>

where there is an additional component varying [[sine wave|sinusoidally]] over space. The wavelength of this variation could be quite large, such as an atomic width. Thus there appear to be several stable potentials around a gravitational force in this model.

==Conformal unification to the Standard Model==
By adding a suitable gravitational term to the [[Standard Model]] action in [[curved space|curved]] [[spacetime]], the theory develops a local conformal (Weyl) invariance. The conformal gauge is fixed by choosing a reference mass scale based on the gravitational constant. This approach generates the masses for the [[vector boson]]s and matter fields similar to the [[Higgs mechanism]] without traditional spontaneous symmetry breaking.<ref>{{citation |first1=M. |last1=Pawlowski |first2=R. |last2=Raczka |year=1994 |title=A Unified Conformal Model for Fundamental Interactions without Dynamical Higgs Field |doi=10.1007/BF02148570 |journal=Foundations of Physics |volume=24 |issue=9 |pages=1305–1327 |arxiv=hep-th/9407137|bibcode = 1994FoPh...24.1305P |s2cid=17358627 }}</ref>
